Collision Risk Animals that collide with a rotating turbine blade may suffer recoverable injuries, injuries that later result in their death, or they may be killed outright. This risk is the most difficult to resolve because it depends on the behavior and swimming capabilities of each species, as well as our limited ability to monitor and detect a rare occurrence [9]. Whether pelagic species are present or at risk is dependent upon site selection. The configuration of a CEC may also be more or less conducive to collisions if it naturally or artificially deters or mitigates contact with marine animals. The MTV does not include any rotating external submerged equipment and, therefore, does not present any potential impact for this consideration. Effects of Underwater Noise The concern around the effects of underwater noise from CECs focuses on marine mammals and certain fish species that use sound extensively for communication and navigation. Systems placed in the water with significant sound sources may attract, deter, or harm sensitive marine animals. Use of the International Electrochemical Commission 62600-40 international specification for measuring underwater sound from marine energy devices [10] provides a pathway for measuring the sound emissions from turbines. Coupled with regulatory thresholds for harm to marine mammals, prepared by NOAA [11] and guidance on harm to fish prepared by BOEM [12], it is possible to assess the likelihood of a particular model of the turbine emitting sound at levels of concern. All turbines measured to date emit operational sound at levels below the thresholds and guidance levels [13]. The MTV’s onboard systems are standard naval sources of sound and should not present any impacts on this consideration. However, CECs and the sites where they might be tested could impact this consideration. Monitoring and analysis (before and during CEC introduction into the natural environment) can effectively predict or confirm the level of this impact, dependent on the present species sensitive to acoustic noise. Effects of Electromagnetic Fields Any power cables that run between the MTV and CECs can generate electromagnetic fields (EMFs). Sensitive marine animals may be adversely affected, particularly those that spend considerable time in close proximity to an EMF source (most commonly benthic organisms). Ongoing research in this area appears to indicate that the levels of EMF carried by small numbers of tidal turbines, with outputs less than 10 MW, are unlikely to be harmful to marine animals [14]. Because power generated by CECs will be limited by MTV power management equipment well below 10 MW, it is not likely that this consideration will impact a CEC, even when an external power export umbilical cable is used. There are no standard methods for measuring EMF or regulatory thresholds.
